full_judgment:
"It is an essential condition of the administration of justice, in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the due process of justice." He submits that the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are not applicable in this case and in both the cases the accused persons appeared and were on bail and then absconded and the appeals were preferred in both the cases within the prescribed period of limitation. But here in this case the petitioner was absconding all along and after the pronouncement of the judgment he was apprehended 3 years after and since he was a fugitive he cannot challenge the proceeding under section 561A of the CrPC. He submits that inherent power of this court does not extend to such jurisdiction which can be exercised by this court in sending the case back on remand for giving an opportunity to the petitioner to cross-examine the witnesses already examined. 

 15. It is now well settled by various Judicial pronouncements of all the Courts of the subcontinent that a fugitive cannot challenge the proceeding against him and there is no denial about this legal proposition. During trial the petitioner was a fugitive and could not file appeal against his conviction and sentence after his arrest as the prescribed period of time of limitation expired. Admittedly the petitioner was apprehended after 3 years and then moved this petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure challenging the trial which was not held in accordance with law. During trial the Tribunal admittedly did not fulfil the requirement of section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act by publishing at least in two Bengali daily newspapers for circulation directing the accused petitioner to appear before it. In sub-section (6) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act, prior to the amendment, it was not mandatory and the word used there was ''may but by amendment of this sub-section (6) the word ''shall'' has been substituted in place of ''may'' making it mandatory. Thus it appears that the trial without such publication and notification was in clear violation of the mandatory provision as enumerated in section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act. It is not an irregularity curable under section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but a glaring illegality. In this case for non-compliance of the mandatory legal requirement before commencement of trial, the accused petitioner had no means to know that he is to appear before a court of law. The submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that it is curable under section 537 of the Code is of no substance. His submission is that a fugitive cannot challenge any Order passed in a judicial proceeding against him. The decision referred by him is not applicable in this case as because during trial he was a fugitive and after arrest challeged the order on the ground of gross illegality and violation of the mandatory provision of law rendering the whole trial vitiated. In the case reported in 1956 (FC) 44 referred by the learned Assistant Attorney General wherein it has been held that essential condition of the administration of justice in a case affecting an individual, that the person concerned should submit to the due process of justice. Here, in this case, when the petitioner is in custody he is not debarred to challenge the impugned judgment and order convicting and sentencing him since he submitted to the due process of justice. We are of the view that as soon as the petitioner is apprehended to serve out the order of conviction and sentence imposed upon him by the trial Court, he cannot be termed as a fugitive and there is no bar for challenging the judgment and order on any point of illegality and legal bar.
